title: Slices Holding All Five Vowels
statement:
You get a lowercase string word. A slice of it (a contiguous, non-empty substring) is fully vowel when it is made only of the letters a, e, i, o, u and each of the five appears at least once.

Return how many fully vowel slices word has. Slices at different positions count separately, even when they spell the same text.

examples.why: "aeiou" and "aeiouu". The slice "eiouu" has no a, so it does not count.
All five vowels appear in the word, but the x splits them, and no slice may contain a consonant.
Inside "aeioua": "aeiou", "aeioua" and "eioua". Slices that start at the b are not allowed.

constraints: word contains only lowercase English letters
hints: A consonant ends every fully vowel slice. Split the word into maximal all-vowel stretches and handle each one on its own.

Fix the right end of a slice. Which left ends work? Moving the left end further left only adds letters, so once a slice contains all five vowels, every slice that starts earlier inside the same stretch does too.

For each right end, remember where each vowel was last seen. The left end can go as far right as the smallest of those five positions, and as far left as the start of the current stretch. That range has a size you can add directly.

explain.intuition:
Fix where a slice ends, at position r. The slice must stay inside the current run of vowels, so it cannot start before start, the first position after the last consonant. It must also reach back far enough to include one copy of every vowel. The latest place it can start is the smallest of the last positions of a, e, i, o, u: start any later and that vowel falls out.

So every start between start and min(last) works, which is min(last) − start + 1 slices, and you get the count for each right end in O(1). It is the same trick as counting windows in a log that contain at least one event of every type.
steps: Keep start (where the current vowel run began) and last[v] for each vowel, all reset when you meet a consonant.
Walk r from left to right. On a consonant, set start = r + 1 and clear last.
If all five vowels have a recorded position, add min(last) − start + 1 to the answer.
pitfalls: Counting distinct slice texts instead of positions. Two equal slices at different places are two answers.
Forgetting to clear the last-seen positions at a consonant. A vowel seen before the consonant cannot be part of a slice that ends after it.
Stopping at the first slice that contains all five vowels for each start. Longer slices that start at the same place also count.

solutions.title: Grow every slice from every start
solutions.idea: For each start, extend to the right while the letters are vowels, tracking which vowels have been seen. Once all five are in, every further extension is another answer.

solutions.title: Last-seen position of each vowel
solutions.idea: For each right end, the valid starts run from the start of the vowel stretch to the oldest of the five last-seen positions.

followups: Count slices that contain exactly k distinct vowels instead of all five. (Hint: at most k minus at most k − 1.)
The alphabet is arbitrary and the required set has m letters. How does the cost change?
lcTitle: Count Vowel Substrings of a String
